posts.headline: BEFORE THE AUDIT: FREEZE THE SCOPE
posts.copy:
Before you claim a freight billing error, establish exactly what you reviewed.

Carrier, mode, date range, legal entity, currencies and exclusions define the starting population. If prior corrections and existing disputes are missing, the same credit can be counted twice.

RETALLY's new printable worksheet makes this starting check practical. The arithmetic is illustrative; it does not prove an overcharge.

posts.headline: BEFORE THE AUDIT: FREEZE THE SCOPE
posts.copy:
A freight audit should start with a denominator—not a dollar sign.

Which carriers, invoice periods, modes and credits are in scope? If those answers change silently, your “savings” figure becomes difficult to defend.

Save this pre-audit checklist. The printable version belongs with the full RETALLY invoice-audit guide, not in your DMs.

posts.headline: TWO BILLS. ONE OBLIGATION?
posts.copy:
Two freight invoices have the same shipment identifier. Is that a duplicate?

Possibly—but a carrier could also have corrected and reissued the bill. Trace the original amount, replacement record, actual payment, posted credit and final obligation before counting a second charge.

Use the printable freight review worksheet to check economic identity first. No refund is implied by matching numbers.

Explore the evidence-first worksheet:

posts.headline: TWO BILLS. ONE OBLIGATION?
posts.copy:
Two invoices for one load can be a duplicate—or a normal correction chain.

Look for the original bill, any replacement, payment and credit memo. Three documents do not necessarily mean three separate obligations.

Save this four-record check before your next freight AP review.

posts.headline: WHICH RATE ACTUALLY APPLIES?
posts.copy:
The lower freight rate is not automatically the correct one.

A defensible review establishes which signed agreement, tariff, amendment or spot quote actually governed the shipment and date. Without that authority, a spreadsheet rate difference is only a question.

Save the source list and work through the printable worksheet before labeling an overcharge.

posts.headline: WHICH RATE ACTUALLY APPLIES?
posts.copy:
Two rate sheets. One shipment.

The lowest number cannot decide the case. Check the signed authority, relevant dates, incorporated tariffs, amendments and corrected bills.

Missing terms are an evidence gap, not money waiting to be recovered. Save this checklist.

posts.headline: 90 MINUTES BILLED. WHAT DO THE TERMS SAY?
posts.copy:
ILLUSTRATIVE EXAMPLE — NOT A CUSTOMER RESULT.

Gate in 08:30 and out 11:00 means 150 minutes onsite. Suppose the applicable written terms give 120 free minutes from arrival without relevant exceptions. Only 30 minutes remain beyond free time. A bill for 90 detention minutes raises a 60-minute question.

Confirm the trigger, appointment provisions, minimums, corrections and credits before asserting an error. The worksheet preserves that evidence decision—not a fake refund estimate.

posts.headline: 90 MINUTES BILLED. WHAT DO THE TERMS SAY?
posts.copy:
ILLUSTRATIVE DETENTION MATH — NOT A CUSTOMER RESULT.

08:30 gate in → 11:00 gate out = 150 minutes onsite.

Hypothetical contract: 120 minutes free from arrival. That leaves 30 minutes beyond free time. If 90 were billed, the 60-minute difference is a question—not a guaranteed overcharge.

Save this example. The commercial terms and prior credits decide.

posts.headline: ALREADY CREDITED? DO NOT COUNT IT TWICE.
posts.copy:
A potential freight discrepancy can already be resolved in the payment ledger.

Before reporting 'new savings,' trace corrected invoices, automatic credits, incumbent auditor work, refunds and later reversals. Prior credits can reduce—or eliminate—the unresolved arithmetic question.

Our browser-only sample worksheet shows this explicitly. It is not a claim that any money has been recovered.

posts.headline: ALREADY CREDITED? DO NOT COUNT IT TWICE.
posts.copy:
ALREADY CREDITED?

A correction that your AP team already received is not a new recovery. Reconcile invoice → replacement → payment → usable credit → any reversal before assigning financial value.

Save this netting check for your next monthly close.

#FreightRecovery #FinanceControls #RETALLY

posts.headline: A FLAG IS NOT A CLAIM.
posts.copy:
Would a second reviewer understand your freight discrepancy without requesting a fresh explanation?

A supportable record links the shipment and invoice, governing commercial terms, service evidence, reproducible calculation and prior credits. That may support a finding; it does not mean the carrier approved it or a refund arrived.

Print the free evidence checklist and document which source is still missing.

posts.headline: A FLAG IS NOT A CLAIM.
posts.copy:
A dashboard flag is not proof of overbilling.

Show the invoice, shipment record, contract version, documented service, repeatable recalculation and existing credits.

If anything essential is missing, label the question unresolved—not recovered. Save the evidence order.

posts.headline: DON'T PUT INVOICES IN DMS.
posts.copy:
Your confidential carrier rate agreement should not be forwarded through Facebook comments or direct messages.

Start with non-sensitive context such as freight mode, carrier types and the period to review. Private invoices, contracts, banking information and credentials must wait for an agreed secure transfer route and appropriate authorization.

The public worksheet accepts only illustrative or anonymized amounts and does not upload them. Share the guide—not your records.

Explore the evidence-first worksheet:

posts.headline: DON'T PUT INVOICES IN DMS.
posts.copy:
Your freight invoice does not belong in an Instagram DM.

Discuss scope first: modes, carriers and billing periods. Keep contracts, account identifiers, payment details and invoice files out of social messages.

The printable worksheet runs locally with illustrative amounts. Never post sensitive records to get a quick answer.

posts.headline: APPROVED DOESN'T MEAN RECOVERED.
posts.copy:
A carrier approves a credit. Has money been recovered?

Not necessarily. Approval, a posted credit memo, a usable account offset, an actual refund and any reversal are different events. A defensible ledger reports only eligible realized net value, subject to the written customer engagement.

The printable review worksheet deliberately stops at unresolved arithmetic. It never labels an estimate a recovery.

posts.headline: APPROVED DOESN'T MEAN RECOVERED.
posts.copy:
“CREDIT APPROVED” IS NOT CASH RECEIVED.

Track the approved claim, usable credit, actual refund and any later reversal separately. Only reconciled, eligible realized value belongs in a recovery total.

Save this distinction for your finance reports. No result is guaranteed.

#TransportationFinance #FreightRecovery #RETALLY
